introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (0765 Pure Maths With Mechanics 1, June 2021, Advanced Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL questions; each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D and only one answer must be marked (if more than one answer is marked the score for that question is zero). Formulae booklets and calculators are allowed. Section A: Pure Mathematics (questions 1 to 35); Section B: Mechanics (questions 36 to 50). Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room.

figures.legende: Fig. 1 (Q39): rectangle ABCD with AB = 10 m and AD = 8 m, particles of 1 kg at A, 2 kg at B, 3 kg at C and 4 kg at D.
Fig. 2 (Q41): distance-time curve x = f(t) with its tangent at t = 3 (point (3, 5)) through E(2, 3) and F(5, 9).

Fig. 3 (Q42): ladder AB (length 2a) against a rough wall (B at the top) and a rough floor (A); forces 6 N up and 9 N horizontal at B, weight 42 N at the middle, 36 N up and 9 N horizontal at A, angle theta at A.

La page de garde indique « ADVANCED LEVEL », « 0765 Pure Maths with Mechanics 1 », JUNE 2021, 7 pages dont la page de garde ; les 50 questions sont présentes, numérotées 1 à 50 (Section A Pure Mathematics : 1 à 35 ; Section B Mechanics : 36 à 50). Aucune clé officielle n'est imprimée : toutes les réponses sont calculées par le transcripteur et recalculées par script.
Aucun QCM n'a été converti en question ouverte : aucune clé imprimée à contester, la bonne valeur est dans une option pour les 50 questions, aucune option en double, figures et tableau lisibles.

Question 44 : la vitesse v = 6t - t^2/2 vaut 10 à t = 2 s et à t = 10 s ; l'accélération vaut alors +4 puis -4 m/s^2. L'option D (4 m/s^2) est la seule compatible (on suppose le premier instant, particule encore en accélération) ; la lecture « -4 » n'est pas une option.

Question 45 : le sujet ne dit pas si A continue ou rebondit après le choc. Avec A continuant (vitesse +0.5), B part à 2 m/s et son énergie cinétique vaut 6 J (option C, e = 1/6). Si A rebondissait (-0.5), on aurait 50/3 J, qui n'est pas une option : lecture « A continue » retenue.

Question 40 : le sujet ne fournit pas g. La tension T = 15 x 4 = 60 N n'en dépend pas ; elle est cohérente avec la particule suspendue pour g = 10 m/s^2 (10 x 10 - T = 10 x 4). Réponse 60 racine de 2 N (option B).
Question 41 : les cotes E(2, 3), F(5, 9) et le point (3, 5) sont lus sur la Fig. 2 (figure nette) ; la tangente passe bien par (3, 5) avec une pente de 2, donc 2 m/s (option B).

Question 42 : les forces sont lues sur la Fig. 3 (6 N vers le haut et 9 N horizontale en B ; 42 N au milieu ; 36 N vers le haut et 9 N horizontale en A). Le bilan des forces est équilibré (36 + 6 = 42 ; 9 = 9) et la lecture est donc cohérente ; l'équation des moments en A donne tan(theta) = 5/3 (option B). Le dessin n'est pas à l'échelle (l'angle tracé paraît plus petit que 59 degrés).
Question 39 : les masses (1, 2, 3, 4 kg en A, B, C, D) et les côtés (AB = 10 m, AD = 8 m) sont lus sur la Fig. 1 ; distance cherchée = 56/10 = 5,6 m (option B).

Question 2 : l'option A est imprimée « Symmetricand reflexive » (espace manquant) ; transcrite « Symmetric and reflexive ». Question 7 : la lecture « minimum » est celle de l'énoncé imprimé ; le minimum de la fraction 2/(3 sin(theta - pi/3) + 5) correspond à sin = 1, d'où 5 pi/6 (option A).

Question 12 : la fonction par morceaux est définie sur [0, 4] avec 2 <= x <= 4 pour la deuxième branche ; la relation f(x) = f(x + 4k) fait de f une fonction de période 4, donc f(15) = f(3) = 9 (option D). Le recouvrement des valeurs en x = 0 et x = 4 (f(0) = 2, f(4) = 12) n'intervient pas.

Question 16 : l'option C « ln y = ln|sec x| + k » est la seule forme exacte de la solution générale (ln|y|, y = C sec x) ; l'option B oublie d'intégrer 1/y. Question 23 : bornes -1 et 2 lues sur le scan ; valeur 3 + ln 4 (option D). Question 24 : l'option D est imprimée « -3 < x <= 3 », transcrite telle quelle.
Question 36 : l'option B est imprimée « 5im s^-1 » (coquille manifeste pour « 5i m s^-1 ») ; transcrite avec un symbole i en gras et l'unité m s^-1, sans incidence sur la réponse D (7i + 2j).
Question 14 : tableau lu sur le scan : x = 0 à 4 ; y = 4, 6, 7, 5, 4 ; règle des trapèzes avec h = 1 : 22 (option B).
Constantes : g = 10 m/s^2 est imposé par la question 47 (seule question qui l'utilise) ; aucune autre constante n'est nécessaire. Les corrigés précisent la valeur retenue.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A: PURE MATHEMATICS**

The vector equation of a line passing through the point $(1,3,4)$ and parallel to the vector $\mathbf i-\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: A line through the point with position vector $\mathbf a$ and parallel to $\mathbf d$ has vector equation $\mathbf r=\mathbf a+\lambda\mathbf d$. Here $\mathbf a=\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+4\mathbf k$ (the point $(1,3,4)$) and $\mathbf d=\mathbf i-\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$, so $\mathbf r=\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+4\mathbf k+\lambda(\mathbf i-\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)$. Option D swaps the point and the direction vector; A and B use a direction vector $-4\mathbf i-2\mathbf k$ which is not parallel to $\mathbf i-\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$ (it has no $\mathbf j$ component), and B also passes through the wrong point $(1,-1,2)$. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: $\mathbf r=\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+4\mathbf k+\lambda(-4\mathbf i-2\mathbf k)$
$\mathbf r=\mathbf i-\mathbf j+2\mathbf k+\lambda(-4\mathbf i-2\mathbf k)$
$\mathbf r=\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+4\mathbf k+\lambda(\mathbf i-\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)$
$\mathbf r=\mathbf i-\mathbf j+2\mathbf k+\lambda(\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+4\mathbf k)$

questions.enonce_markdown: A binary relation $R$ is defined on $\mathbb N$, the set of natural numbers, by $m\,R\,n \Leftrightarrow m+n$ is odd. $R$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: *Reflexive?* $m\,R\,m$ would need $m+m=2m$ to be odd, which is never true, so $R$ is not reflexive. *Symmetric?* $m+n=n+m$, so $m\,R\,n\Rightarrow n\,R\,m$: $R$ is symmetric. *Transitive?* If $m+n$ and $n+p$ are both odd, then $m$ and $p$ both have the parity opposite to that of $n$, so they have the same parity and $m+p$ is even: for example $1\,R\,2$ and $2\,R\,3$ but not $1\,R\,3$. So $R$ is not transitive. *Anti-symmetric?* This needs ($m\,R\,n$ and $n\,R\,m\Rightarrow m=n$); but $1\,R\,2$ and $2\,R\,1$ with $1\neq2$, so $R$ is not anti-symmetric. Hence $R$ is symmetric only. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that the roots of the equation $x^2-14x+k=0$ are $m$ and $n$ and that $3m=4n$, the value of the constant $k$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The sum of the roots is $m+n=14$ and the product is $mn=k$. From $3m=4n$ we get $m=\tfrac43 n$, so $\tfrac43 n+n=\tfrac73 n=14$, giving $n=6$ and $m=8$. Check: $3\times8=24=4\times6$. Then $k=mn=8\times6=48$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The gradient of the tangent to the curve with parametric equations $x=\dfrac2t$ and $y=3t$, where $t$ is a parameter, at the point where $t=1$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\dfrac{2}{t^2}$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=3$. Then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{3}{-2/t^2}=-\dfrac{3t^2}{2}$. At $t=1$ the gradient is $-\dfrac32$. The trap is to invert the quotient ($\dfrac{dx/dt}{dy/dt}$), which gives $-\dfrac23$ (option A). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The range of values of $x$ for which $|x|>2-|x|$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Add $|x|$ to both sides: $2|x|>2$, so $|x|>1$. This means $x>1$ or $x<-1$. Check: $x=2$ gives $2>0$ (true), $x=0$ gives $0>2$ (false), $x=-2$ gives $2>0$ (true). Options B and D are the opposite (inside) intervals, and C results from the error $|x|>2$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When a polynomial function $f(x)$ is divided by $x-1$, the quotient is $2x^2+x-2$ and the remainder is $3$. The polynomial $f(x)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Dividend $=$ divisor $\times$ quotient $+$ remainder, so $f(x)=(x-1)(2x^2+x-2)+3$. Expand: $(x-1)(2x^2+x-2)=2x^3+x^2-2x-2x^2-x+2=2x^3-x^2-3x+2$. Adding the remainder: $f(x)=2x^3-x^2-3x+5$. Check: $f(1)=2-1-3+5=3$, the remainder. Option A forgets to add the remainder $3$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of $\theta$ for which $\dfrac{2}{3\sin\left(\theta-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+5}$ is minimum is
questions.corrige_markdown: The numerator is constant and positive, and the denominator $3\sin\left(\theta-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+5$ lies between $2$ and $8$, so it is always positive. The fraction is smallest when the denominator is largest, that is when $\sin\left(\theta-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=1$. Then $\theta-\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{\pi}{2}$, so $\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{5\pi}{6}$, and the minimum value is $\frac28=\frac14$. (The maximum occurs when $\sin=-1$, i.e. $\theta=-\frac{\pi}{6}$, which is not an option.) **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The set of values of $x$ for which $(x-1)(x-3)(2x+1)>0$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The critical values are $x=-\tfrac12,\ 1,\ 3$. The cubic has positive leading coefficient ($2x^3+\dots$), so it is positive for $x>3$; the sign alternates at each simple root: negative on $(1,3)$, positive on $\left(-\tfrac12,1\right)$, negative for $x<-\tfrac12$. Check with $x=0$: $(-1)(-3)(1)=3>0$ (inside $\left(-\tfrac12,1\right)$); $x=2$: $(1)(-1)(5)=-5<0$. So the solution is $-\tfrac12<x<1$ or $x>3$. Option A forgets the interval between $-\tfrac12$ and $1$ and takes the wrong sign on the left. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $y=x^{\sin x}$, where $x>0$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Use logarithmic differentiation. Take natural logarithms: $\ln y=\sin x\,\ln x$. Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ (product rule on the right): $\dfrac1y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos x\ln x+\dfrac{\sin x}{x}$. Hence $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\left(\cos x\ln x+\dfrac{\sin x}{x}\right)y$. Options A and C use the power rule as if the exponent were constant; B has a sign error on the first term. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Let $\mathbf A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\d&e&f\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf B=\begin{pmatrix}m&n\\p&q\\r&s\end{pmatrix}$. The order of the matrix product $\mathbf{AB}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $\mathbf A$ has order $2\times3$ and $\mathbf B$ has order $3\times2$. The product $\mathbf{AB}$ is defined because the number of columns of $\mathbf A$ ($3$) equals the number of rows of $\mathbf B$ ($3$), and the product has as many rows as $\mathbf A$ ($2$) and as many columns as $\mathbf B$ ($2$): order $2\times2$. (The product $\mathbf{BA}$ would be $3\times3$, option C.) **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The number of arrangements of the letters of the word $MANNA$ in which the $A$'s are together is
questions.corrige_markdown: Treat the two $A$'s as one block $[AA]$. We then arrange four objects $M,\ [AA],\ N,\ N$, of which the two $N$'s are identical: $\dfrac{4!}{2!}=12$. (Exhaustive listing of the $5!/(2!\,2!)=30$ arrangements confirms that exactly $12$ have the two $A$'s adjacent.) Option A comes from forgetting the factor for the block position; B from taking $3!$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2+2, & 0\le x<2\\ 3x, & 2\le x\le 4\end{cases}$ Given that $f(x)=f(x+4k)$, where $k\in\mathbb Z$, $f(15)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: The relation $f(x)=f(x+4k)$ says that $f$ is periodic with period $4$. Reduce $15$ to the interval $[0,4]$ by subtracting multiples of $4$: $15=3+4\times3$, so $f(15)=f(3)$. Since $2\le3\le4$, use the second branch: $f(3)=3\times3=9$. Option A evaluates $3\times15$ directly, B uses the first branch at $3$ ($3^2+2=11$). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
If the statements $p$ and $q$ are

$p$ : John is eating,

$q$ : John is playing,

the proposition $\sim q\rightarrow p$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The symbol $\sim q$ means "not $q$" = "John is not playing", and $A\rightarrow B$ reads "if $A$ then $B$". So $\sim q\rightarrow p$ is "If John is not playing then he is eating". Option A is $p\rightarrow\sim q$ and B is $p\rightarrow q$ (the antecedent and consequent are swapped); C is $\sim q\rightarrow\sim p$ (the consequent is wrongly negated). **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: If John is eating then he is not playing
If John is eating then he is playing
If John does not play then he will not eat
If John is not playing then he is eating

questions.enonce_markdown:
Values of $y$ for various values of $x$ are as shown in the table.

| $x$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 4 | 6 | 7 | 5 | 4 |

Using the trapezium rule $\displaystyle\int_0^4 y\,dx\approx$
questions.corrige_markdown: There are $5$ ordinates, so $4$ strips of width $h=1$. Trapezium rule: $\int_0^4 y\,dx\approx\dfrac h2\left[y_0+y_4+2(y_1+y_2+y_3)\right]=\dfrac12\left[4+4+2(6+7+5)\right]=\dfrac12(8+36)=22$. Option C is the value of the bracket (the factor $\tfrac h2$ was forgotten) and D applies the Simpson factor $\tfrac h3$ to the trapezium bracket. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The variables $x$ and $y$ are related by the law $y=a^2b^x$. Reducing this law to linear form gives
questions.corrige_markdown: Take logarithms of both sides: $\log y=\log(a^2b^x)=\log a^2+\log b^x=2\log a+x\log b$. This is $Y=mX+c$ with $Y=\log y$, $X=x$, gradient $m=\log b$ and intercept $c=2\log a$. Option C swaps the roles of $a$ and $b$; D treats $b^x$ as $x^b$; B misapplies $\log a^2$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The general solution of the differential equation $\cos x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y\sin x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Separate the variables: $\dfrac1y\,dy=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx=\tan x\,dx$. Integrate: $\ln|y|=\int\tan x\,dx=-\ln|\cos x|+k=\ln|\sec x|+k$. Thus $\ln y=\ln|\sec x|+k$ (equivalently $y=C\sec x$ with $C=\pm e^{k}$). Options A and D use $\int\tan x\,dx=\sec^2x$, which is false ($\frac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^2x$); B forgets to integrate $\frac1y$ into $\ln y$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The sum $S_n$, of the first $n$ terms of a sequence, is $S_n=n(1+2n)\ln2$. The $5^{\text{th}}$ term of the sequence is
questions.corrige_markdown: The $n$th term is $u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$. $S_5=5\times11\ln2=55\ln2$ and $S_4=4\times9\ln2=36\ln2$, so $u_5=55\ln2-36\ln2=19\ln2$. (In general $u_n=\left[n(2n+1)-(n-1)(2n-1)\right]\ln2=(4n-1)\ln2$, and $u_5=19\ln2$.) Option C is the sum $S_5$ of the first five terms, not the fifth term, and A is $S_1$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that the equation $4x^2-3kx+1=0$ has equal roots and $k>0$, the value of the constant $k$ is equal to
questions.corrige_markdown: Equal roots require the discriminant to be zero: $(-3k)^2-4(4)(1)=9k^2-16=0$, so $k^2=\dfrac{16}{9}$ and $k=\pm\dfrac43$. Since $k>0$, $k=\dfrac43$. Check: $4x^2-4x+1=(2x-1)^2$ has the repeated root $x=\tfrac12$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equation of the circle with centre at the point $(1,3)$ and passing through the point $(2,7)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The radius is the distance from the centre $(1,3)$ to $(2,7)$: $r^2=(2-1)^2+(7-3)^2=1+16=17$. The equation is $(x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=17$. Check: the point $(2,7)$ gives $1+16=17$. Option C puts the point on the circle as the centre, A swaps $x$ and $y$ in the centre. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\dfrac{2x-3}{(x-3)(x-2)}\equiv\dfrac{P}{x-3}+\dfrac{Q}{x-2}$, the values of $P$ and $Q$ are respectively
questions.corrige_markdown: Multiply by $(x-3)(x-2)$: $2x-3\equiv P(x-2)+Q(x-3)$. Put $x=3$: $3=P(1)$, so $P=3$. Put $x=2$: $1=Q(-1)$, so $Q=-1$. Check at $x=0$: $-3=3(-2)+(-1)(-3)=-6+3=-3$. The sign of $Q$ is the usual trap (option D). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The range of values of $x$ for which $\dfrac{x+3}{x}>0$, $x\neq0$, is
questions.corrige_markdown: The quotient is positive when numerator and denominator have the same sign. Both positive: $x+3>0$ and $x>0$, so $x>0$. Both negative: $x+3<0$ and $x<0$, so $x<-3$. Hence $x<-3$ or $x>0$. (Equivalently, $x(x+3)>0$ since multiplying by $x^2>0$ preserves the inequality.) Option A is the set where the quotient is negative. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equation of a circle with end-points $(4,-2)$ and $(3,2)$ of its diameter is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a circle with diameter end-points $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ the equation is $(x-x_1)(x-x_2)+(y-y_1)(y-y_2)=0$ (the angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so the vectors from a point $(x,y)$ to the two end-points are perpendicular). With $(x_1,y_1)=(4,-2)$ and $(x_2,y_2)=(3,2)$: $(x-4)(x-3)+(y+2)(y-2)=0$. Check that $(4,-2)$ satisfies it: $0+0=0$. Options B, C and D mix up the coordinates ($y_1=-2$ must appear as $y+2$). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{2}\frac{3+x}{2+x}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Write $\dfrac{3+x}{2+x}=1+\dfrac{1}{2+x}$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{2}\left(1+\frac1{2+x}\right)dx=\Big[x+\ln|2+x|\Big]_{-1}^{2}=(2+\ln4)-(-1+\ln1)=3+\ln4\approx4.386$. The integrand is continuous on $[-1,2]$ because $2+x>0$ there. Numerical check: the average value of the integrand is about $1.46$ over an interval of length $3$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The expansion of the function $\dfrac{1}{(1-3x)(1+x)}$ is valid for
questions.corrige_markdown: The binomial series for $(1-3x)^{-1}$ converges for $|3x|<1$, that is $-\tfrac13<x<\tfrac13$, and the one for $(1+x)^{-1}$ for $|x|<1$. The product (or the partial-fraction expansion) is valid where both are valid, which is the more restrictive condition $-\tfrac13<x<\tfrac13$. The end-points are excluded (strict inequalities): at $x=\tfrac13$ the function is not even defined, so option A is wrong. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Cartesian equation of the curve whose parametric equations are $x-1=\sec\theta$ and $y+1=\tan\theta$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Use the identity $\sec^2\theta-\tan^2\theta=1$: $(x-1)^2-(y+1)^2=1$. Expand: $x^2-2x+1-y^2-2y-1=1$, so $x^2-y^2-2x-2y-1=0$. This is a rectangular hyperbola with centre $(1,-1)$. Check with $\theta=0$: $x=2$, $y=-1$ gives $4-1-4+2-1=0$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}6&k&2\\4&-3&3\\2&-k&2\end{pmatrix}$ is not invertible (i.e. is singular), the value of $k$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: A square matrix is singular exactly when its determinant is zero. Expand along the first row: $\det=6\big[(-3)(2)-(3)(-k)\big]-k\big[(4)(2)-(3)(2)\big]+2\big[(4)(-k)-(-3)(2)\big]=6(-6+3k)-2k+2(6-4k)=-36+18k-2k+12-8k=8k-24$. Setting $8k-24=0$ gives $k=3$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int2x\,(x^2+3)^{\frac32}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Let $u=x^2+3$, so $du=2x\,dx$. Then $\int u^{3/2}\,du=\dfrac{u^{5/2}}{5/2}+k=\dfrac25u^{5/2}+k=\dfrac25(x^2+3)^{5/2}+k$. Check by differentiating: $\dfrac25\cdot\dfrac52(x^2+3)^{3/2}\cdot2x=2x(x^2+3)^{3/2}$. Option A forgets to divide by $\tfrac52$ properly (it uses $\tfrac15$) and D multiplies by $\tfrac52$ instead of dividing. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A first approximation to the root of the equation $e^x+2x-1=0$ is $x=1$. Using the Newton-Raphson method, a second approximation to the root of the equation is
questions.corrige_markdown: Let $f(x)=e^x+2x-1$, so $f'(x)=e^x+2$. Newton-Raphson: $x_{n+1}=x_n-\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$. With $x_1=1$: $f(1)=e+2-1=e+1$ and $f'(1)=e+2$. So $x_2=1-\dfrac{e+1}{e+2}\approx1-0.788=0.212$. Option B inverts the fraction, C uses $f(1)=e-1$ (sign slip on the constant), D adds instead of subtracting. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equation $x^3+3x-5=0$ has a root lying in the open interval
questions.corrige_markdown: Let $f(x)=x^3+3x-5$, which is continuous. $f(-1)=-9$, $f(0)=-5$, $f(1)=1+3-5=-1<0$, $f(2)=8+6-5=9>0$, $f(3)=31$. The sign changes between $x=1$ and $x=2$, so by the intermediate value theorem there is a root in $(1,2)$. (Since $f'(x)=3x^2+3>0$, $f$ is increasing and this is the only real root.) **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $|z-3|=2|z+3|$, where $z=x+iy$, the locus described by $z$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Square both sides: $|z-3|^2=4|z+3|^2$, i.e. $(x-3)^2+y^2=4\left[(x+3)^2+y^2\right]$. Expand: $x^2-6x+9+y^2=4x^2+24x+36+4y^2$, so $3x^2+3y^2+30x+27=0$, i.e. $x^2+y^2+10x+9=0$, or $(x+5)^2+y^2=16$. This is a circle with centre $(-5,0)$ and radius $4$ (a circle of Apollonius: the ratio of the distances to $3$ and $-3$ is not $1$). A line would appear only for the ratio $|z-3|=|z+3|$ (the $y$-axis). **Answer: A.**
Use $e^{\ln5}=5$ and the index law $e^{x\ln5}=\left(e^{\ln5}\right)^x=5^x$. Check with $x=2$: $e^{2\ln5}=e^{\ln25}=25=5^2$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The approximate change in the value of $\ln x$ if $x$ changes from $10$ to $10.1$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a small change $\delta x$, $\delta y\approx\dfrac{dy}{dx}\,\delta x$. With $y=\ln x$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac1x$, so $\delta(\ln x)\approx\dfrac1{10}\times0.1=0.01$. Exact value: $\ln10.1-\ln10=\ln1.01=0.00995\approx0.01$. Option A is the change in $x$ itself. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The vectors $2\mathbf i-q\mathbf j-\mathbf k$ and $-3\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+q\mathbf k$ are perpendicular if the scalar $q$ is equal to
questions.corrige_markdown: Two vectors are perpendicular when their scalar (dot) product is zero: $(2)(-3)+(-q)(-2)+(-1)(q)=-6+2q-q=q-6=0$, so $q=6$. Check: $(2,-6,-1)\cdot(-3,-2,6)=-6+12-6=0$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The vector perpendicular to the plane $3x-5y+z+7=0$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a plane $ax+by+cz+d=0$ the vector $a\mathbf i+b\mathbf j+c\mathbf k$ is normal (perpendicular) to the plane. Here $a=3$, $b=-5$, $c=1$, so the normal is $3\mathbf i-5\mathbf j+\mathbf k$. The constant $7$ only fixes the position of the plane and does not enter the normal (options A, C and D include it). **Answer: B.**

Use $\tan(P+Q)=\dfrac{\tan P+\tan Q}{1-\tan P\tan Q}$ with $\tan P=5$ and $\tan Q=-3$: $\tan A=\dfrac{5-3}{1-(5)(-3)}=\dfrac{2}{16}=\dfrac18$. Numerical check: $\tan^{-1}5\approx1.3734$ and $\tan^{-1}(-3)\approx-1.2490$, so $A\approx0.1244$ and $\tan A\approx0.125$. The trap is the sign in the denominator: using $1+\tan P\tan Q=-14$ gives $-\tfrac17$ (option D). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B: MECHANICS**

The position vector of a particle is $\mathbf r=\left[(t^3+2t^2+2)\mathbf i+(t^2-1)\mathbf j\right]$ m at time $t$ s. The velocity of the particle when $t=1$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Velocity is the derivative of the position vector: $\mathbf v=\dfrac{d\mathbf r}{dt}=(3t^2+4t)\mathbf i+2t\,\mathbf j$. At $t=1$: $\mathbf v=(3+4)\mathbf i+2\mathbf j=(7\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Option C, $(10\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)$, is the acceleration $\mathbf a=(6t+4)\mathbf i+2\mathbf j$ at $t=1$ (derivative taken twice). **Answer: D.**

themes: elastic strings and potential energy mechanics
questions.enonce_markdown: When the length of a spring is $60\%$ of its natural length, the thrust in the spring is $10\ \mathrm N$. The modulus of the spring is
questions.corrige_markdown: Let the natural length be $l$. The compressed length is $0.6\,l$, so the compression is $x=0.4\,l$. Hooke's law for a spring in compression: thrust $T=\dfrac{\lambda x}{l}=\dfrac{\lambda(0.4\,l)}{l}=0.4\,\lambda$. With $T=10\ \mathrm N$: $\lambda=\dfrac{10}{0.4}=25\ \mathrm N$. The trap is to use the length $0.6\,l$ instead of the compression $0.4\,l$, which gives $\lambda=\tfrac{50}{3}\ \mathrm N$ (option A). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A centripetal force of $72\ \mathrm N$ causes a particle of mass $4\ \mathrm{kg}$ to move in a horizontal circle of radius $2\ \mathrm m$. The angular speed of the particle is
questions.corrige_markdown: The centripetal force is $F=m\omega^2r$, so $\omega^2=\dfrac{F}{mr}=\dfrac{72}{4\times2}=9$ and $\omega=3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. Options C and D have the unit of a linear speed, which is wrong for an angular speed (the linear speed would be $v=\omega r=6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$); A forgets the square root. **Answer: B.**

themes: centre of mass of composite bodies
questions.enonce_markdown:
Fig. 1 below shows four particles placed at the vertices of rectangle $ABCD$.

![fig-1](gce-al-pm-mechanics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

Fig. 1

The distance of the center of gravity from the side $AB$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: From Fig. 1: $AB=10$ m, $AD=8$ m; masses $1$ kg at $A$, $2$ kg at $B$, $3$ kg at $C$, $4$ kg at $D$. Take $AB$ as the $x$-axis. The distances of the particles from $AB$ are $0$ ($A$), $0$ ($B$), $8$ m ($C$) and $8$ m ($D$). Total mass $=1+2+3+4=10$ kg. Distance of the centre of gravity from $AB$: $\bar y=\dfrac{1(0)+2(0)+3(8)+4(8)}{10}=\dfrac{56}{10}=5.6\ \mathrm m$. The trap is to take the geometric centre of the rectangle ($4$ m, option A), which ignores the unequal masses. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle of mass $15\ \mathrm{kg}$ rests on a smooth horizontal table. It is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table to a particle of mass $10\ \mathrm{kg}$ which hangs freely. Given that the acceleration of the system is $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ when it is released from rest, the force exerted by the string on the pulley is
questions.corrige_markdown: Let $T$ be the tension in the string (same on both sides, because the pulley is smooth and the string light). The $15$ kg particle moves horizontally on a smooth table, so the only horizontal force on it is $T$: $T=15\times4=60\ \mathrm N$ (this does not need $g$; the hanging particle gives the same result, $10g-T=10\times4$, i.e. $T=60\ \mathrm N$ for $g=10$). The string pulls on the pulley with two forces of magnitude $T$: one horizontal (towards the particle on the table) and one vertical (downwards, towards the hanging particle). They are perpendicular, so the resultant force on the pulley is $\sqrt{60^2+60^2}=60\sqrt2\ \mathrm N\approx84.9\ \mathrm N$, directed at $45^\circ$ below the horizontal. Option C is the tension alone. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
![fig-2](gce-al-pm-mechanics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

Fig. 2

Fig. 2 shows a sketch of the distance-time graph of a particle whose distance $x$ m from a fixed point at time $t$ s is given by $x=f(t)$. The tangent to the curve at $t=3$ is shown passing through two distinct points $E$ and $F$. The speed of the particle when $t=3$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: On a distance-time graph the gradient of the tangent is the instantaneous velocity $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$. The tangent at $t=3$ passes through $E(2,3)$ and $F(5,9)$, so its gradient is $\dfrac{9-3}{5-2}=\dfrac{6}{3}=2$. Hence the speed at $t=3$ is $2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Consistency check: the tangent also passes through the marked point $(3,5)$ of the curve, since from $E$ it rises $2\times1=2$ over one second ($3+2=5$). The trap is to use the coordinates of the touching point, $x/t=5/3$, or of $F$, which are not gradients. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A uniform ladder $AB$, of length $2a$, rests in limiting equilibrium with its top end against a rough vertical wall and its lower end on a rough horizontal floor. The forces acting on the ladder are as shown in Fig. 3 below.

![fig-3](gce-al-pm-mechanics-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

Fig. 3

The angle $\theta$ which $AB$ makes with the floor is given by
questions.corrige_markdown:
Forces read on Fig. 3: at $B$ (top, on the wall) a normal reaction $9\ \mathrm N$ horizontal (away from the wall) and a friction force $6\ \mathrm N$ upwards; the weight $42\ \mathrm N$ downwards at the midpoint $G$; at $A$ (on the floor) a normal reaction $36\ \mathrm N$ upwards and a friction force $9\ \mathrm N$ horizontal towards the wall. Check of the resultant force: vertically $36+6=42$ (equal to the weight) and horizontally $9=9$, so the forces balance. Take moments about $A$ (length $AB=2a$, the ladder makes angle $\theta$ with the floor). The horizontal distance from $A$ to the line of action of the weight is $a\cos\theta$. The point $B$ is at horizontal distance $2a\cos\theta$ and height $2a\sin\theta$ from $A$, so the $9\ \mathrm N$ force at $B$ has moment arm $2a\sin\theta$ and the $6\ \mathrm N$ force at $B$ has moment arm $2a\cos\theta$. The weight turns the ladder one way and the two wall forces turn it the other way: 

$$
42\,a\cos\theta=9\,(2a\sin\theta)+6\,(2a\cos\theta)
$$

This gives $42\cos\theta-12\cos\theta=18\sin\theta$, i.e. $30\cos\theta=18\sin\theta$, so $\tan\theta=\dfrac{30}{18}=\dfrac53$ ($\theta\approx59.0^\circ$). Option D, $\sin\theta=\tfrac53$, is impossible since $\sin\theta\le1$. The trap is to ignore the vertical friction at the wall ($6\ \mathrm N$ at $B$), which would give $42\cos\theta=18\sin\theta$ and $\tan\theta=\tfrac73$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The velocity of $X$ is $(4\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Relative to $X$ the velocity of $Y$ is $(3\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and relative to $Y$ the velocity of $Z$ is $(5\mathbf i-3\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The true velocity of $Z$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Relative velocity: $\mathbf v_{Y/X}=\mathbf v_Y-\mathbf v_X$ and $\mathbf v_{Z/Y}=\mathbf v_Z-\mathbf v_Y$. Adding: $\mathbf v_Z=\mathbf v_X+\mathbf v_{Y/X}+\mathbf v_{Z/Y}=(4\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)+(3\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)+(5\mathbf i-3\mathbf j)=(12\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Intermediate step: $\mathbf v_Y=(7\mathbf i+7\mathbf j)$ (option C is the true velocity of $Y$, not $Z$). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle accelerating from rest has its speed $v\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at time $t$ s given by $v=6t-\tfrac12t^2$. The acceleration of the particle when $v=10$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Acceleration is $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=6-t$. Find the time(s) when $v=10$: $6t-\tfrac12t^2=10\iff t^2-12t+20=0\iff(t-2)(t-10)=0$, so $t=2$ or $t=10$. At $t=2$ s: $a=6-2=4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (the particle is still speeding up). At $t=10$ s the acceleration is $-4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, i.e. a retardation of magnitude $4$ (the particle is then slowing down, having passed its maximum speed of $18\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $t=6$). The value $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ is the only one that matches the options. Option B, $10$, is the speed, not the acceleration. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A smooth sphere $A$ of mass $4\ \mathrm{kg}$ travelling at $5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ collides directly with another smooth sphere $B$ of mass $3\ \mathrm{kg}$ travelling at $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in the opposite direction. Given that the speed of $A$ after impact is $0.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the kinetic energy of $B$ after impact is
questions.corrige_markdown: Take the initial direction of motion of $A$ as positive. Conservation of linear momentum: $4(5)+3(-4)=4v_A+3v_B$, i.e. $8=4v_A+3v_B$. If $A$ continues in its original direction ($v_A=+0.5$): $3v_B=8-2=6$, so $v_B=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (in the direction of $A$'s original motion). Then the kinetic energy of $B$ is $\tfrac12(3)(2)^2=6\ \mathrm J$. Consistency check: the coefficient of restitution is $e=\dfrac{v_B-v_A}{u_A-u_B}=\dfrac{2-0.5}{5-(-4)}=\dfrac16$, which lies between $0$ and $1$; kinetic energy before $=\tfrac12(4)(25)+\tfrac12(3)(16)=74\ \mathrm J$, after $=\tfrac12(4)(0.25)+6=6.5\ \mathrm J$, so energy is lost as it must be in an inelastic collision. (If $A$ rebounded, $v_A=-0.5$, one would get $v_B=\tfrac{10}{3}$ and $\tfrac{50}{3}\ \mathrm J$, which is not an option.) Option D, $6.5\ \mathrm J$, is the total kinetic energy after impact, not that of $B$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The work done by a force $\mathbf F=(\mathbf i-2\mathbf j-4\mathbf k)\ \mathrm N$ which moves its point of application from a point $A$ with position vector $\mathbf r_A=(3\mathbf i-4\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$ to another point $B$ with position vector $\mathbf r_B=(-\mathbf i+6\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Work done $=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d$ where $\mathbf d=\mathbf r_B-\mathbf r_A=(-\mathbf i+6\mathbf k)-(3\mathbf i-4\mathbf k)=-4\mathbf i+10\mathbf k$ m. Then $W=(1)(-4)+(-2)(0)+(-4)(10)=-4-40=-44\ \mathrm J$. The negative sign means that the force opposes the displacement overall. Reversing the displacement ($\mathbf r_A-\mathbf r_B$) gives $+44$ (option D). **Answer: B.**

themes: motion of a vehicle with resistance
questions.enonce_markdown: The engine of a car of mass $1{,}200\ \mathrm{kg}$ works at a constant rate of $54\ \mathrm{kW}$ up a road inclined at an angle $\sin^{-1}\left(\frac15\right)$ to the horizontal. Given that the non-gravitational resistance to the motion of the car is $300\ \mathrm N$ and taking $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the maximum speed of the car is
questions.corrige_markdown: At maximum speed the acceleration is zero, so the driving force $F$ balances the resistance plus the component of the weight down the slope: $F=300+mg\sin\alpha=300+1200\times10\times\tfrac15=300+2400=2700\ \mathrm N$. Power $P=Fv$, so $v=\dfrac{P}{F}=\dfrac{54\,000}{2700}=20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Using only the weight component gives $22.5$ and using only the resistance gives $180$; neither is an option. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A coin is biased in such a way that the probability of it landing head-up is $\dfrac34$. The coin is tossed $3$ times, the probability of getting exactly one tail is
questions.corrige_markdown: Let $X$ be the number of tails in $3$ tosses: $X\sim B\left(3,\tfrac14\right)$ (the probability of a tail is $1-\tfrac34=\tfrac14$). $P(X=1)=\dbinom31\left(\dfrac14\right)\left(\dfrac34\right)^2=3\times\dfrac14\times\dfrac9{16}=\dfrac{27}{64}\approx0.422$. Option A forgets the factor $3$ for the position of the tail. **Answer: C.**

themes: centre of mass of composite bodies
questions.enonce_markdown: Two particles of masses $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $3\ \mathrm{kg}$ are placed at the points $(3,1)$ and $(8,6)$ respectively. The position of their center of mass is at the point
questions.corrige_markdown: The centre of mass has coordinates $\bar x=\dfrac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}=\dfrac{2(3)+3(8)}{5}=\dfrac{30}{5}=6$ and $\bar y=\dfrac{2(1)+3(6)}{5}=\dfrac{20}{5}=4$. So it is at $(6,4)$, nearer to the heavier particle. Option B is the unweighted midpoint $(5.5,3.5)$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A force of $14\ \mathrm N$ acts on a particle of mass $70\ \mathrm{kg}$ causing the speed of the particle to increase from $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to $7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The distance travelled by the particle during this period is
questions.corrige_markdown: Newton's second law: $a=\dfrac Fm=\dfrac{14}{70}=0.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Using $v^2=u^2+2as$: $49=9+2(0.2)s$, so $0.4\,s=40$ and $s=100\ \mathrm m$. Work-energy check: $Fs=\tfrac12m(v^2-u^2)$ gives $14s=35\times40=1400$, so $s=100\ \mathrm m$. Option A ($40$) is the value of $v^2-u^2$. **Answer: D.**
